units.translation: In the following verses (3 fr. 12 J.) he also speaks about the death of Acrisius, that after the petrification of Polydectes and those with him by the head of the Gorgon [in Seriphos], Perseus leaves Dictys in Seriphos to rule over the remaining Seriphians, while he himself sailed to Argos with the Cyclopes and Danae and Andromeda; and when he arrived he did not find Acrisius in Argos, for he had withdrawn in fear of him to the Pelasgians at Larissa. Not finding him, he leaves Danae with her mother Eurydice, and Andromeda and the Cyclopes, and went himself to Larissa, and upon arriving he recognizes Acrisius and persuades him to follow to Argos. And when they were about to go, they happen upon a contest of young men in Larissa, and Perseus strips for the contest and taking the discus throws it; for the pentathlon did not exist then, but they competed in each of the contests separately. The discus, rolling, strikes Acrisius on the foot and wounds him. Suffering from this, Acrisius dies there in Larissa; and Perseus and the Larisaeans bury him before the city, and the locals make a hero-shrine for him. Perseus then departs from Argos.

1093-95a. Echetus the insolent: Homer mentions Echetus as most cruel, but Arete as having happened in her time; for she says "not even far off." We found the story in the catalogue of impious men attributed to Lysippus of Epirus.

b. "bronze in the dark": the order is "in a dark hut."
c. "bronze sinning" is also written "bronze erring." P
1100. "But I fear to transgress justice" Lᵐ (P)
1125. "Hyllic": from Hyllus, son of Melite and Heracles. Lᵐ (P)

1131. "in a holy cave": in the great and divine one, in which Macris dwelt. In this cave she nursed Dionysus [which is called Dithyrites]. Because of this Dionysus was called Dithyrambus, because the cave has two doors. Lᵐ (P)
1136-38. "And Hera, angered, drove Macris out of Euboea because she received Dionysus from Hermes and nursed him. Euboea is sacred to Hera."
1141. "There then they spread": in the cave of Macris, he says, the marriage of Medea and Jason took place, but Philetas in his Telephus (fr. 9 Kuchenmueller) says it was in the house of Alcinous.

1146-48. "Shame held each": through these he says that the nymphs, desiring to touch the fleece because of its beauty, nevertheless out of shame refrained because the union was to take place upon it. Concerning the fleece, that it was golden most relate, but Acusilaus in his Genealogies (2 fr. 37 J.) says it was dyed purple by the sea.
